title: The Clay of the Tardenois to the Pauper's Row: Camille Claudel, Sculptor
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Fere-en-Tardenois, birth in the registrar's town
stops.date_confidence: attested; civil registry of the commune
stops.campa: On the eighth of December, in the wheat country north of Paris, a daughter is born to Louis-Prosper Claudel, registrar of mortgages, and Louise-Athanaise Cerveaux. They name her Camille Rosalie. An elder brother, Charles-Henri, died in infancy the year before, and the mother has not finished mourning him; the child who arrives instead is not the child she wanted. The birth is entered in the register like any other birth in the commune. A registrar's career will move this household through half a dozen small towns before it reaches Paris, and she will take nothing out of the Aisne but the clay in its fields.
suggested_refs: The civil registry of Fere-en-Tardenois, Aisne, entry of 8 December 1864

stops.name: Villeneuve-sur-Fere, the first figures
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the family holds property here through these years, but no single summer is documented
stops.campa: The family keeps property at Villeneuve-sur-Fere, a hamlet of farms and quarries, and here the children spend their earliest years and every summer of their childhood. Camille digs clay out of the fields and makes figures of it, untaught, before anyone has told her that this is a thing a person can do for a living. Her mother disapproves; her father, watching, does not stop her. Her brother Paul is born in this village in August 1868 and will spend his life writing about the sister who could not stop putting faces into mud.
suggested_refs: The Claudel family property at Villeneuve-sur-Fere, Aisne
sources: Musee Camille Claudel, Nogent-sur-Seine, biographical materials

stops.name: Bar-le-Duc, the first transfer
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the posting; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Louis-Prosper is transferred to Bar-le-Duc in the Meuse, and the household packs. Camille is not yet six. The town gives her nothing the record keeps: no teacher, no exhibited work, no anecdote beyond the fact of residence. What it gives her is the pattern of the whole childhood. The father's office is reassigned every few years and the mother and three children follow it. Camille learns to pack her own work and carry it to the next provincial address, since nothing else in the arrangement stays where it is put.
suggested_refs: The mortgage registry office of Bar-le-Duc, Meuse
sources: standard biographical chronologies of the Claudel family

stops.name: La Montagne, the escarpment above the village
stops.date_confidence: traditional only; neither the years nor the exact site is documented, and this pin is placed beside the village rather than surveyed
stops.campa: Above Villeneuve rises a broken limestone ridge the villagers call La Montagne, wind-cut outcrops a girl can climb and roam alone. Family memory holds that she takes the clay for her earliest figures from its foot, and that the rock itself, not any master, first teaches her what mass is and what a cavity does to it. No document fixes the spot. The claim survives in the recollections of relatives and in Paul Claudel's later writing, which returns to this hillside whenever it has to account for his sister at all.
suggested_refs: The limestone outcrops called La Montagne, above Villeneuve-sur-Fere
sources: Family tradition as reported by Reine-Marie Paris
Paul Claudel's writings on his sister

stops.name: Nogent-sur-Seine, the sculptor next door
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The family settles at Nogent-sur-Seine, and here, at twelve, Camille meets Alfred Boucher, a working sculptor who lives nearby, who took a second prix de Rome and failed twice at the first, and who looks at a child's clay studies and sees work rather than a pastime. He corrects her modeling. He treats her as a student. The first adult to tell her that the work is serious happens to live in the town the ministry has sent her father to, and everything she does afterward runs out of that posting.
suggested_refs: Alfred Boucher's studio at Nogent-sur-Seine, and his instruction of the twelve-year-old Claudel
sources: Musee Camille Claudel, Nogent-sur-Seine, official history

stops.name: Wassy-sur-Blaise, the last provincial address
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Another transfer, and the Claudels are in Wassy in the Haute-Marne for the next post. Camille is fifteen and already impossible about sculpture, modeling wherever the family lands, indifferent to how unlikely a town is as a place to become an artist. Wassy leaves no surviving work and no story beyond residence. It is the last address chosen for her by someone else's employer, and she spends it arguing, in a house where only her father agrees with her, that the next move has to be to Paris.
suggested_refs: The Claudel household at Wassy, Haute-Marne, 1879 to 1881
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Paris, the household at 135 bis boulevard du Montparnasse
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted. Sources differ on who drove the move: fr.wikipedia has the mother bringing the children to Paris, while biographers credit the father's insistence against his wife's wishes
stops.campa: The family takes an apartment on the boulevard du Montparnasse, in the quarter where the sculptors' studios cluster, so that Camille, sixteen, can pursue sculpture properly. Louis-Prosper stays behind in the provinces for his work and supports from a distance a household he will rarely live in. Louise-Athanaise, who wanted none of this, keeps house in a city she did not choose for a daughter she does not understand. The arrangement makes the career possible, and it ends the marriage in everything except law.
suggested_refs: 135 bis boulevard du Montparnasse, the Claudel family's first Paris address, 1882 to 1886
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Academie Colarossi, the school that admits women
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The Ecole des Beaux-Arts does not admit women to its sculpture ateliers, so she enrolls on the rue de la Grande-Chaumiere at the Academie Colarossi, one of the few Paris schools that will put a female student in front of a live model. She works there beside a small cohort of women, several of them English, with an intensity the teachers still recall decades afterward. The academy gives her the training the state withholds. It is a workaround and not a welcome, and she uses it as one, without gratitude and without complaint.
stops.quote: When you left on Saturday, I felt a horrible void, I saw you everywhere, on the beach, in your room, in the garden.
stops.quote_source: A letter of Camille Claudel's, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002); the addressee is not named in the passage and the seaside setting fits her English correspondence rather than Rodin
suggested_refs: The Academie Colarossi, rue de la Grande-Chaumiere, and its admission of women to life modeling

stops.name: Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs, the shared studio
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month approximate
stops.campa: She rents a studio at 117 rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs with several young English sculptors, Jessie Lipscomb among them, and Alfred Boucher comes regularly to criticize the group's work for nothing. The room is cold and crowded, and it belongs to them and to nobody senior. Her closest correspondence in these years runs to England, to Florence Jeans, in letters the two women agree to destroy as they arrive. She submits to the Salon des Artistes Francais from this address, including a bust of the family's old servant known as Vieille Helene.
stops.quote: Don't fear anything for your letters, they are burnt one by one and I hope you do the same with mine.
stops.quote_source: Camille Claudel to Florence Jeans, February, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002)
suggested_refs: 117 rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs, the studio shared with Jessie Lipscomb and other English sculptors
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Depot des marbres, entering Rodin's studio
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Boucher leaves for Italy and asks a friend to take over the criticism of his students. The friend is Auguste Rodin, and by the following year Camille is working in his atelier at the Depot des marbres on the rue de l'Universite as a praticienne, one of the hands that execute his monumental commissions. She carves for the Burghers of Calais and models figures for the Gates of Hell, the doorway Rodin is building out of Dante's Inferno, so that her thumbs go into a poem six hundred years dead. Two years after Boucher hands her over she is cutting work that leaves the studio under another man's name.
suggested_refs: Rodin's atelier at the Depot des marbres, 182 rue de l'Universite
The Gates of Hell campaign and the praticiens who executed it
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: 31 boulevard de Port-Royal, the liaison
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the residence years 1886 to 1892; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: She takes rooms at 31 boulevard de Port-Royal, and the working relation with Rodin has become the other thing as well. He is twenty-four years older and has lived with Rose Beuret since before Camille was born. The letters that survive from these years are not the letters of an assistant. She writes to him about absence and about other women, in a hand that assumes she has the standing to demand an accounting, and for roughly a decade she does have it, in every room but the one he goes home to.
stops.quote: I sleep completely naked to make me believe you are here, but when I wake up it is not the same thing.
stops.quote_source: Camille Claudel to Auguste Rodin, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002)
suggested_refs: 31 boulevard de Port-Royal, Claudel's Paris address 1886 to 1892, now marked with a commemorative plaque
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Folie Neubourg, the studio behind the wall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the address recurs in letters and biographies, the building was demolished, and sources differ on the precise pavilion
stops.campa: Rodin secures her a private studio in a half-ruined eighteenth-century folly off the boulevard d'Italie, the Folie Neubourg, its garden run wild and its rooms unheated. Here she works alone on her own commissions, out of sight of his official atelier and the men in it who compare every piece she makes to his. What she develops in these rooms is what critics will later call unmistakably hers, figures at small scale caught mid-gesture instead of posed. The building does not survive; the address does.
suggested_refs: The Folie Neubourg, also called Clos Payen, boulevard d'Italie, since demolished
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Palais de l'Industrie, Sakuntala and the honorable mention
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; the honorable mention is tagged as reconstruction in the source pool. Salon opening month approximate
stops.campa: At the Salon des Artistes Francais in the Palais de l'Industrie she shows Sakuntala, two figures in marble folded into each other at the moment of recognition, and takes an honorable mention. The same year she models a bust of Rodin, which is to say she makes her master sit for her. The Salon jury is the only gate open to a woman with no state academy behind her, and she goes through it without scandal, still read by the critics who notice her as an extension of the studio she works in rather than a rival to it.
suggested_refs: Sakuntala, marble, exhibited at the Salon des Artistes Francais
Claudel's bust of Auguste Rodin, 1888
sources: Salon des Artistes Francais exhibition records as cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Chateau de l'Islette, the summers on the Indre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summers of 1890, 1891 and 1892; exact months of residence not fixed
stops.campa: Rodin rents the Chateau de l'Islette on the Indre, in the commune of Cheille, and the two of them spend three summers there away from Paris and away from Rose Beuret. The owners remember Camille working outdoors in the garden. What is documented as made here is La Petite Chatelaine, the head of the owner's granddaughter, cut several times over, a child's face with the hair worked into a weight the neck can barely hold. It is the last stretch of the relationship in which the word for what she is doing is still work rather than defense.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de l'Islette at Cheille, rented by Rodin for the summers of 1890, 1891 and 1892
La Petite Chatelaine, in its several versions
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Paris, the end of the liaison
stops.date_confidence: contested; fr.wikipedia dates the definitive separation to 1892, with Rodin choosing to remain with Rose Beuret, while en.wikipedia has the two continuing to see each other until 1898. The contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: After an abortion she ends the intimate side of it. Rodin does not leave Rose Beuret; he will marry her thirty-five years later, two weeks before she dies. Whether the two of them go on seeing each other for six more years or stop within the season is a thing the sources say differently and no document settles. Claude Debussy, who is close to Camille in these years, describes the end of his own attachment to her in a phrase that outlives every account of it. She keeps working. She stops signing herself anyone's student.
stops.quote: I weep for the disappearance of the Dream of this Dream.
stops.quote_source: Claude Debussy on the end of his relationship with Camille Claudel, quoted in Victor I. Seroff, Debussy: Musician of France (Books for Libraries Press, 1970), p. 152
suggested_refs: The 1892 separation and the disputed date at which contact between Claudel and Rodin ceased
sources: Victor I. Seroff, Debussy: Musician of France (1970)

stops.name: Champ-de-Mars, Clotho at the Societe Nationale
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Salon opening month approximate
stops.campa: She exhibits Clotho at the Salon of the Societe Nationale des Beaux-Arts on the Champ-de-Mars, an old woman stripped to the bone and tangled in the thread she is spinning, and she is working on La Valse, a man and a woman locked together as though falling rather than dancing. The account that the jury refuses to authorize a nude version for state purchase and requires her to clothe the figures is repeated everywhere and rests on correspondence cited but not printed. Nothing in either piece resembles an assistant's work.
suggested_refs: Clotho, exhibited 1893 at the Salon of the Societe Nationale des Beaux-Arts
La Valse, in its draped and undraped states
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Direction des Beaux-Arts, the marble commissioned
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of the commission; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The Direction des Beaux-Arts commissions a marble of L'Age mur: a man pulled away from a kneeling young woman by an older one who already has him by the shoulder. Everyone who sees it reads it as Rodin, Rose Beuret, and Camille, whatever she says. The commission is granted, then stalled, then cancelled in 1899. That Rodin intervened to kill it is the version her family will hold to for a century; the documentary trail for his hand in it is thinner than the story, and her biographers say so plainly.
suggested_refs: The 1895 state commission for a marble L'Age mur and its cancellation in 1899
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Meudon, the house she is not in
stops.date_confidence: attested that Rodin acquires the Villa des Brillants in 1895; no dated visit by Claudel is recorded here
stops.campa: Rodin buys the Villa des Brillants above the Seine at Meudon and settles his life visibly around Rose Beuret in it, workshop and household under one roof. Camille almost certainly never enters it. It is the household she is refused and the arrangement she is not part of, and it will go on standing there long after she can be reached by anything. Biographers place the final cooling of the relationship in these years without producing a single dated scene that happens at Meudon at all.
suggested_refs: The Villa des Brillants at Meudon, Rodin's house and workshop from 1895
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Champ-de-Mars, L'Age mur and the withdrawal of support
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Salon month approximate
stops.campa: Rodin sees L'Age mur and reacts with shock and anger, taking the group for what everyone takes it for, an account of how he left her, put permanently into bronze at public scale. He withdraws his support. In the same year the state commission for the marble quietly lapses. She has made the one work that cannot be read as his and has been charged for it at the only rate the art world of 1899 collects from a woman: the loss of the man whose name opened every door she had been walking through for sixteen years.
suggested_refs: L'Age mur, plaster and bronze states, and Rodin's reaction to it
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, the studio on the Ile Saint-Louis
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of the move; month approximate
stops.campa: She rents studio and apartment at 19 quai de Bourbon in the Hotel de Jassaud on the Ile Saint-Louis, overlooking the Seine, and moves in alone. This is her address for fourteen years. She works here prolifically and downward in scale, small bronzes that a dealer can actually sell, Les Causeuses, La Vague in onyx and bronze, four women bent together under a breaking wave. The monumental marble the state was going to pay for is not coming, so she works to the market that does exist, in pieces a private apartment can hold.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Jassaud, 19 quai de Bourbon, Ile Saint-Louis, Claudel's studio and residence 1899 to 1913
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Exposition Universelle, a bronze medal
stops.date_confidence: the medal is tagged as reconstruction in the source pool; the date given is the opening of the Exposition, not of the award
stops.campa: Paris fills with the fair, and in the crush of national pavilions and prize juries Camille Claudel takes a bronze medal at the Exposition Universelle. Rodin, refused adequate space inside, has built his own pavilion at the Place de l'Alma and is the most famous sculptor alive. She is forty minutes' walk away with a medal and no commission, exhibiting inside a system that will award her a distinction and not buy the work. After this year her public standing and her private condition stop matching each other, and the gap only widens.
suggested_refs: The 1900 Exposition Universelle prize lists
Rodin's private pavilion at the Place de l'Alma, 1900

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, Persee et la Gorgone
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of completion; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: She completes Persee et la Gorgone: the hero holding the severed head high and away, looking not at it but past it, since to meet that face is to be turned to stone. Visitors to the quai in these years find her at the block herself, with the dust on her, refusing the practice universal in her trade of handing the marble to a hired carver. It is professional pride and it is also an argument. Half of Paris has spent twenty years saying that the good passages in her work are really Rodin's, and she answers with her own hands.
stops.quote: You find me at work; excuse the dust on my blouse.
stops.quote_source: Camille Claudel to a studio visitor, reported in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002); the remark continues, 'I sculpt my marble myself'
suggested_refs: Persee et la Gorgone, marble, completed 1902
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Galerie Eugene Blot, the exhibition that comes too late
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year; exact opening day not established
stops.campa: The dealer Eugene Blot mounts a show of her work on the boulevard de la Madeleine, bronzes cast from her plasters, La Valse and L'Implorante among them, and the notices are real: Octave Mirbeau and others write about her as an artist standing free of Rodin at last. It is the high point of her public career. It is also within months of its close. The same year her patron the comtesse de Maigret breaks with her. Blot will keep casting and defending her for decades, one of the last people outside her family to behave as though she is still there.
stops.quote: A revolt against nature: a woman genius.
stops.quote_source: Octave Mirbeau on Camille Claudel, quoted in 'Camille Claudel, une icone au destin tragique,' Connaissance des Arts, 2 July 2020
suggested_refs: The Galerie Eugene Blot exhibition of December 1905
Blot's bronze casts of La Valse and L'Implorante
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, the shutters
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year the seclusion begins; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Paul marries and leaves for a posting in China, and the studio closes around her. She boards the windows. She refuses visitors, her mother included. She goes days without eating and destroys her own work in bouts she describes afterward as defense, since the thefts are constant and the thieves are Rodin's. Neighbors report her talking to herself behind the shutters. The letters she writes in these years are lucid in their grammar and impossible in their content, and they are the letters her family will later hand to a doctor.
stops.quote: Last night, two men tried to force my shutters. I recognized them: they are two of Rodin's Italian models. He told them to kill me.
stops.quote_source: Camille Claudel, letter, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002)
suggested_refs: Claudel's persecution letters of the quai de Bourbon years
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)
family correspondence cited in Reine-Marie Paris

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, the Seine in the studio
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; the date given is the crest of the great Paris flood
stops.campa: The river comes up over the quais and into the ground floors of the Ile Saint-Louis, and her studio is damaged in the great flood. Plaster does not survive water. Whatever the boarded windows had been keeping safe, the Seine reaches anyway, and the woman who has spent four years convinced that her work is being taken from her by night watches a good part of it destroyed by the city itself in a single week. She does not leave the apartment. There is nowhere in Paris she is still willing to go.
suggested_refs: The great flood of the Seine, January 1910, and the damage on the Ile Saint-Louis

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, breaking the plasters
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted. No source counts what was destroyed
stops.campa: She breaks her plasters. Models, studies, unsold work, smashed in the studio and carted off, in what biographers describe as the destruction of most of her life's output, though nobody counts and nobody can. What survives survives because a dealer had already cast it in bronze or a collector had already taken it away. The catalogue raisonne that will be compiled eighty-four years later lists what came through this room, not what went out of it in pieces. She has one more year at this address.
suggested_refs: The 1912 destruction of Claudel's plasters at the quai de Bourbon

stops.name: Villeneuve-sur-Fere, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: sources differ by a day; en.wikipedia gives 3 March, other biographies 2 March
stops.campa: Louis-Prosper Claudel dies at Villeneuve-sur-Fere, the one member of the family who had defended his daughter's vocation from the beginning and her liberty at the end. Camille is not told in time to attend the funeral; by several accounts the news is deliberately held back until after the burial. His death removes the last obstacle between her and the arrangement her mother has wanted for years. Eight days separate the funeral of the man who moved a household to Paris for her and the morning they come for her.
suggested_refs: The grave of Louis-Prosper Claudel at Villeneuve-sur-Fere
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Paris, Dr Michaux signs the certificate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Five days after the death, a physician named Michaux certifies that Camille Claudel is suffering serious mental disturbance. French law of 1838 requires a doctor's certificate and a family member's request, and the family has both. She is not examined in any way she consents to and is not told what the paper is for. Michaux will still be receiving her letters four years later, from six hundred kilometres away, asking him to undo what he signed in a single morning in Paris on the seventh of March.
suggested_refs: The medical certificate of 7 March 1913 and the French confinement law of 1838

stops.name: 19 quai de Bourbon, taken away
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the tenth of March orderlies come to the quai de Bourbon and take her. She does not resist, according to their report. She leaves the boarded windows, the surviving sculptures, and the accumulated evidence of fourteen years of work, and she does not set foot in Paris again for the thirty years that are left to her. The apartment is cleared soon after and almost nothing in it is preserved. Rodin's friend Mathias Morhardt says in public what the art world says privately about the brother who arranged it.
stops.quote: Paul Claudel is a simpleton. When one has a sister who is a genius, one doesn't abandon her. But he always thought he was the one who had genius.
stops.quote_source: Mathias Morhardt, quoted in Arline Boucher Tehan, The Gates of Hell: Rodin's Passion in Stone, ch. 3 (Xlibris, 2010)
suggested_refs: The clearing of the quai de Bourbon studio, March 1913
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)
Arline Boucher Tehan, The Gates of Hell (2010)

stops.name: Ville-Evrard, the first asylum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the hospital register
stops.campa: She is admitted the same day to Ville-Evrard at Neuilly-sur-Marne, a public asylum east of Paris, at her brother's request, with none of the comfort the family could have paid for. She writes constantly from here to Paul, to old friends, to the doctor who signed, protesting her sanity and demanding release, and the letters are filed. The diagnoses in the surviving record do not agree with each other: persecution mania in some notes, dementia praecox in others. The disagreement is part of the record and has never been resolved.
suggested_refs: The Ville-Evrard admission register, 10 March 1913
Eric Favereau's Liberation investigation of the Claudel confinement papers
sources: Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (2002)

stops.name: Montdevergues, transferred south
stops.date_confidence: three French sources give 12 February 1915, including the Ville-Evrard register, which records her resident there from 10 March 1913 to that date; en.wikipedia gives 7 September 1914, with an admittance certificate dated 22 September 1914. The English date is the outlier and is recorded, not adopted
stops.campa: With the war on the Marne and Ville-Evrard emptied for the wounded, she is moved the length of the country to the asylum of Montdevergues at Montfavet, outside Avignon. The distance is itself a further sentence. Her brother's postings take him abroad for years at a stretch and the journey from Paris is a day each way, so that visits which were already rare become almost theoretical. The admittance paperwork records what she is being held for in the vocabulary the century has for women who will not be quiet.
stops.quote: from a systematic persecution delirium mostly based upon false interpretations and imagination
stops.quote_source: Certificate of admittance, Montdevergues asylum, dated 22 September 1914, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002), p. 210
suggested_refs: The Montdevergues admittance certificate
The wartime evacuation of Ville-Evrard

stops.name: Montdevergues, the letter to Dr Michaux
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Four years in, she writes to the physician who certified her in Paris and asks him to obtain her liberation. The letter is orderly, argued, and addressed to the one man in the chain whose signature could be withdrawn. Nothing comes of it. She will write hundreds more over the coming decades, to her mother, to her brother, to doctors, insisting on the same two points: that she is not mad, and that she wants to go home to work. The asylum files them. Her family, receiving them, treats them as symptoms of the condition they describe.
suggested_refs: Claudel's asylum correspondence, 1913 to 1943

stops.name: Montdevergues, the doctor writes to the mother
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Dr Brunet, the asylum physician, writes to Louise-Athanaise Claudel to say that her daughter could be reintegrated into family life. The mother refuses to take her back. The institution holding her says she does not need to be held; the family says she does. She has been inside seven years at this point and has twenty-three left, and every one of them rests on a letter her mother answered no to. Nothing in the surviving file suggests the offer is ever made again.
suggested_refs: Dr Brunet's 1920 letter proposing Claudel's release

stops.name: Montdevergues, Jessie Lipscomb comes
stops.date_confidence: one source records a first visit in 1924 and another a visit in December 1929; both are retained and neither is preferred
stops.campa: Jessie Lipscomb, who shared the cold studio on the rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs with her forty-seven years earlier, travels down from England to see her, and her husband photographs the two women sitting side by side in the asylum grounds. Lipscomb says afterward, to anyone who asks and to some who do not, that Camille Claudel is not insane. She has no standing to have her released and does not obtain it. The photograph survives, which is more than survives of most of what passed between them.
suggested_refs: William Elborne's 1929 photographs of Claudel and Jessie Lipscomb at Montdevergues

stops.name: Montdevergues, the news of her mother's death
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year of the death; day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Louise-Athanaise Claudel dies in June without ever having visited her daughter, nine years after refusing to take her home. Her sister Louise makes the journey to Montfavet exactly once in her life, in this same year. The tally at the end will be that of everyone who could have opened the door for her, the mother came never, the sister once, and the brother between seven and twelve times in thirty years, depending which account is believed. The refusal outlives the woman who made it by fourteen years.
suggested_refs: The death of Louise-Athanaise Claudel, June 1929

stops.name: Montdevergues, her brother visits
stops.date_confidence: one of the visits listed by en.wikipedia (1913, 1920, 1925, 1927, 1933, 1936, 1943); fr.wikipedia counts twelve visits in all. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Paul Claudel comes down from wherever the diplomatic service has him, sits with his sister, and writes about it afterward in the journals that will be published as literature. He is by now a celebrated poet and an ambassador. He records that she is aged, that she talks about the thefts, that he is moved. He does not take her out. He refuses her the sculpting materials the doctors suggest, and she refuses them too, saying she will not work in a place that is not her own; on this one point brother and sister are in perfect agreement.
suggested_refs: Paul Claudel's journal entries on his visits to Montdevergues

stops.name: Montdevergues, the last October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: She dies on the nineteenth of October, seventy-eight years old, of a stroke, in the fourth year of the occupation and the thirty-first of her confinement, in a hospital where the wartime rations have been killing the inmates by degrees for two years. No relative is present. She has been inside this institution longer than she was ever a sculptor. What she wrote from here about the arithmetic of it has been quoted ever since by people who mostly do not know that the accounting was correct.
stops.quote: What was the point of working so hard and of being talented, to be rewarded like this? Never a penny, tormented all my life.
stops.quote_source: Camille Claudel, asylum correspondence, quoted in Odile Ayral-Clause, Camille Claudel: A Life (Abrams, 2002)

Mortality at French asylums under the occupation

segments.name: The Unclaimed Grave and the Long Return

stops.name: Montfavet cemetery, the pauper's row
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the month; the exact day of burial is not established
stops.campa: She is buried within days in the carre des indigents, the paupers' section, with hospital staff present and no family. Nobody renews the concession. Within roughly a decade the plot is reclaimed for reuse and her remains are moved to a communal ossuary, so that there is now no grave of Camille Claudel anywhere that a person could stand in front of. Her biographers treat this as the last act of the same decision taken in March 1913, carried through to its conclusion by the simple method of not paying a bill.
suggested_refs: The carre des indigents of the Montfavet cemetery and the communal ossuary

stops.name: Musee Rodin, the first retrospective
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Paul Claudel, eighty-two and four years from his own death, organizes a retrospective of some forty of his sister's works. He holds it in the museum named for Auguste Rodin, which is the only institution in France with a serious holding of her sculpture, in part because Rodin himself kept and preserved her pieces through the years when nobody else would. The rehabilitation of her name begins in the house of the man she spent the last forty years of her life accusing of having destroyed it.
suggested_refs: The 1951 Claudel retrospective at the Musee Rodin, Hotel Biron

stops.name: Villeneuve-sur-Fere, a plaque over nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: A plaque reading Camille Claudel, 1864-1943 is unveiled in the cemetery of the village where she spent every summer of her childhood and where her father is buried. There are no remains beneath it and everyone present knows it. It is a marker for a body in an ossuary six hundred kilometres south, put up by a village that remembers a girl digging clay out of its fields, a hundred and four years after she was born and twenty-five after she died in a place none of them ever went.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque of 28 September 1968, cemetery of Villeneuve-sur-Fere

stops.name: Musee d'Orsay, the state buys L'Age mur
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of acquisition; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The French state purchases a bronze of L'Age mur, cast posthumously from her plaster, eighty-eight years after commissioning the marble and eighty-four after letting the commission lapse. It now stands in one of the most visited rooms in Paris: the man being pulled away, the young woman on her knees with her hands still out. The following year a retrospective travels from the Musee Rodin to Poitiers, and two years after that Anne Delbee's book puts her back into the language of a country that had mislaid her.

stops.name: Paris, the film that makes her famous
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the French release; the two Academy Award nominations followed at the ceremony held in 1990, not 1989, though the five Cesars were won in 1989
stops.campa: Bruno Nuytten's film opens with Isabelle Adjani in the part, and within a year Camille Claudel is better known to the general public than she was at any moment of her life. Five Cesars, then two Academy Award nominations. What the film fixes in the popular mind is the tormented genius destroyed by a great man and a cold family, which is true enough in outline and flattens the thirty asylum years into silence. Her surviving letters from Montfavet are lucid, furious, and entirely unlike the myth built on top of them.

Anne Delbee, Une femme (1982)

stops.name: Montfavet cemetery, the cenotaph
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Her great-niece Reine-Marie Paris, who has spent decades collecting and writing about her, has a cenotaph erected in the cemetery at Montfavet, sixty-five years after the burial and half a century after the plot was cleared. She says plainly what it is for: the family forgot Camille on purpose, and this is an attempt at repair by the only branch of it still interested in making one. It marks memory rather than a body. There is no longer any body it could mark.
suggested_refs: The 2008 cenotaph at Montfavet, erected by Reine-Marie Paris

stops.name: Buenos Aires, two borrowed works
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the loan is reported but no exhibition catalogue, museum record, or period press notice was located to corroborate it, and month and day are unknown
stops.campa: L'Implorante and La Vague, which Argentines see billed as La Ola, are shown at the Museo Nacional de Arte Decorativo, lent from museum collections in Mexico and Puerto Rico. They stay a season and go home. No work of hers is bought, and none is held in any Argentine collection before or after. Rodin is all over this city in bronze, in the Parque Tres de Febrero and on the Plaza del Congreso and by the roomful at the Bellas Artes; his praticienne comes once, on loan, for a few weeks, and leaves nothing behind.

stops.name: Nogent-sur-Seine, the museum in the Maison Claudel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of opening
stops.campa: A museum devoted to her opens in the eighteenth-century house at Nogent-sur-Seine where the family lived, in the town where Alfred Boucher first told a twelve-year-old that her clay was work. It shows about half of her roughly ninety surviving sculptures, more of her than stands anywhere else. The circuit her father's postings opened in 1876 closes here, a hundred and forty-one years later, in the one provincial town on the whole itinerary that had ever given her anything, and the house has her name on it rather than his.
suggested_refs: The Musee Camille Claudel, Nogent-sur-Seine, opened 26 March 2017 in la Maison Claudel
